text: CITY ATTORNEY'S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE E CITY CLERK'S OFFICE
(Word Count: 496)
This measure was placed on the ballot by an initiative petition signed by the requisite number of Redwood City registered voters. It requires a majority for passage.
This measure would repeal Chapter 42 of. the Municipal Go±e and replace it with an identically numbered chapter that would include the following changes:

Rent Control: Current law caps annual rent increases to between 5% and 10%, depending on the percentage change in local inflation, on specified rental units 15 years old or older. Current law also exempts single-family homes, condominiums, and housing built after February 1, 1995, from local rent control.

This initiative would impose rent control on specified units built before February 1 1995, by capping the base rent rate to the amount paid on October. 29» 2025 (for units occupied on that date) orto the initial rent rate (for units occupied after that date). Annual base rent rate increases would be capped at the rate equal to 60% of the percentage increase in local inflation and no more than 5%. Separately, both landlords and tenants could petition the City for an increase or decrease in rent under certain circumstances.

Evictions and Relocation Assistance: Under current law, after 12 months of tenancy in certain types of residential properties, landlords can evict tenants only for certain reasons, known as just cause. Just cause includes both evictions where the tenant is at fault (e.g., failure to pay rent) and evictions through no fault of the tenant (e.g., owner move-in). For no- fault evictions, tenants are entitled to relocation assistance equal to at least one month of the tenant's rent, while qualifying low-income and families with special circumstances are entitled to more. And in certain instances, after a no-fault eviction, a tenant has the right to return to the rental unit.

This initiative would extend just cause protections to single-family homes, ADUs, and deed- restricted affordable housing, and mobile homes. tt would impose more restrictions against both at-fault and no-fault evictions, including additional notice requirements and specific rules for elderly and disabled tenants and for households with children or educators during the school year. It would extend the right to return to any tenant after a no-fault eviction if the rental unit is returned to the rental market by the landlord or a successor landlord. And for no-fault evictions, the initiative would require landlords to provide relocation assistance equal to 4 times the monthly U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development fair market rent or $12,000, whichever is greater, while elderly and disabled tenants would receive an additional $6,000.

Miscellaneous Provisions: The initiative would also require landlords to submit tenant safety plans for City approval before performing repairs or renovations; regulate "buyout" offers that induce vacancy; prohibit landlords from taking specified actions in bad faith; and pro.vide civil remedies, including treble damages, for violations.

New City Responsibilities: The initiative would require the Cityto set annual rent increases; hear rent petitions, review tenant safety plans; issue regulations; and set and collect an annual fee on landlords to pay for administering the initiative.
The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure E. If you desire a copy of the measure, please call the City Clerk's Office at (650) 780-7220 and a copy will be mailed at no cost to you.
Veronica Ramirez, City Attorney City of Redwood City

text: Mom and pop landlords, homeowners, and longtime Redwood City renters all agree: Rent control will keep Redwood City affordable and create stability for our community.

Corporate landlords and real estate trusts have bought up 87% of multifamily housing in Redwood City, and rents have skyrocketed. Our children can't find housing here. Our teachers, city employees, and essential workers live far away and commute for hours.

Residents are getting rent hikes of $350 a month, which may be higher once the temporary 10% state rent cap expires. Families are forced out by unjust evictions, intimidation, or health problems from neglected repairs. Seniors are at risk of homelessness.
With Measure , Redwood City will join 30+ cities around California that have enacted fair rent control and meaningful renter protections, including Mountain View and East Palo Alto,

Measure will: Keep costs stable by allowing predictable rent increases of 60% of inflation or 5%, whichever is lower. Guarantee landlords a fair return on their investment—if costs increase, a landlord can petition the city for a larger rent increase. Only allow evictions if there is a "just cause" (e.g. failure to pay rent, breach of lease, owner moving into the unit). Protect against landlord use of intimidation and lack of repairs to push people out of their homes. Prevent homelessness through higher relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.
Measure _ will be funded by a small fee on landlords—not paid for by homeowners, renters, nor the city's general fund.

Measure was drafted by a diverse group of Redwood City residents who've been working for a decade to keep families and seniors in their homes, so our community can be safe and strong. Over 7,000 Redwood City voters signed petitions to get Measure on the ballot.
Join all of us, your neighbors, and vote YES on Measure to keep Redwood City affordable!

text: The Redwood City Council voted 6-0 to oppose Measure 7
Me.asure _ was not prepared by the City Council or City staff. The measure repeals strong tenant protection measures adopted by the Redwood City Council that exceed State laws protecting renters.
Redwood City is committed to protecting renters. Many of us are renters ourselves, and our families have lived with the instability this measure claims to address.

But good intentions don't guarantee good policy. If approved by voters, Measure _ will mean less affordable housing, higher prices for renters, and new costs to the City likely impacting essential city programs and services.

An independent, City-commissioned analysis found this measure would cost Redwood City up to $11 million per year and require up to 18 new full-time employees to administer. The initiative prohibits the City from using General Fund dollars, but the math does not work.

Cuts to critical neighborhood services or new taxes will be needed to fund ongoing implementation. Whatis worse, this initiative targets non-profit affordable housing projects, single-family homes and in-law units with onerous regulations and fees.

Nonprofit housing providers would face new fees, unsustainable rent restrictions, and tightening operating budgets. This will drain funds needed for repairs, resident services, and long-term preservation of the affordable housing this measure claims to protect.
As a citizens' initiative, any future changes to the ordinance will require a costly city-wide election.

text: Small housing providers, affordable housing nonprofits, small businesses, first responders and the Redwood City Council oppose Measure E for the same underlying reasons: Measure E's unintende consequences will put essential City programs and services at risk, and reduce housing affordability and choice.

Measure E is costly. Two independent financial analyses found administering this program cou d cost up to $11 million per year and require 18 new full-time employees. Fees could reach $757 per rental unit with the gap diverted from other Citv departments, such as police and fire. This is not a "small fee."

Measure E is a sharp departure from other cities by not exempting affordable housing nonprofits. Nonprofits like the St. who have spent decades providing and preserving affordable homes, would face the same fees as corporate landlords, threatening their ability to maintain buildings and fund resident services.

Measure E applies to every apartment, single family home, in-law and nonprofit affordable housing unit in Redwood City. It requires between in relocation payments to move back in, or renovate your home. Any change or fix to Measure E requires another costly citywide election.

With no General Fund backstop, an unproven program with an $11 million price tag could mean real cuts to police, fire and services our neighborhoods depend on. This measure risks our safety net and the affordable housing it claims to protect.
Don't trade affordable housing, City services and safe neighborhoods for a flawed measure.
Vote NO on Measure E.

text: It's unfortunate our City Council is defending the interests of corporate landlords instead of responding to the needs of Bedwood City residents.
We've spent the past decade pleading with the Redwood City Council to address the affordability crisis. But they've chosen not to pass meaningful protections.
The facts are:
MeasureS will keep 6,300+ apartments affordable for Redwood City families and increase housing stability for 40,000 neighbors.

Measure E will NOT cost Redwood City taxpayers anything, as it will be funded by a small per-unit fee on landlords. Measyre E prohibits use of the general fund for its ongoing costs, so why would the City Council raise taxes or cut city services? Corporate landlords, who own most of our rental housing, will pay the largest share of the fees. This works in many other California cities, and it will work for us.
Measure E regulates landlords — NOT ordinary homeowners. And small landlords who rent out single-family homes are exempt from rent control under state law.
Measure E will NOT impact building affordable housing. State law exempts all units built after 1995 from rent control, meaning there's no impact on building any new housing.
Like any landlord, nonprofits that own the few subsidized apartments built before 1995 can petition for a higher rent increase if needed.

Don't be fooled. Corporate landlords and real estate trusts have bought up 87% of apartments in Redwood City. They are spending big money to defeat Measure E to protect their profits, not to "protect affordable housing." RECEIVED Vote YES on Measure E: Keep Redwood City affordable.

Jill Ohline, Small Landlord Geogina Castaneda, Affordable Housing Resident Maria Garcia, Homeowner Abigail Korman, teacher Kyla Valenti, Benefits Analyst II, County of San Mateo (signed in her individual capacity only)
